name: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
significance: Built hand-ground single-lens microscopes and was the first person to observe and describe bacteria, protozoa, and sperm cells, calling them animalcules.

name: Robert Koch
significance: Formulated Koch's postulates and identified the causative agents of anthrax, tuberculosis, and cholera; awarded the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

name: Louis Pasteur
significance: Disproved spontaneous generation, developed pasteurization, and created vaccines for anthrax and rabies.

name: Alexander Fleming
significance: Discovered penicillin in 1928 after noticing mold contamination killed nearby bacteria on a culture plate.

name: Alexandre Yersin
significance: Isolated the plague bacillus in Hong Kong during the Third Plague Pandemic in 1894.

name: Kitasato Shibasaburo
significance: Obtained the first pure culture of the tetanus bacillus and co-developed the diphtheria antitoxin with Emil von Behring.

name: Filippo Pacini
significance: First described the cholera-causing comma-shaped bacterium in 1854, decades before it gained wide scientific acceptance.

name: Barry Marshall
significance: Co-discovered Helicobacter pylori and famously drank a culture of it to prove it causes stomach ulcers; shared the 2005 Nobel Prize.

name: Robin Warren
significance: Co-discovered Helicobacter pylori with Barry Marshall, overturning the belief that stress and acid alone caused ulcers.

name: Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran
significance: First observed the malaria parasite in a patient's blood in 1880; awarded the 1907 Nobel Prize.

name: Carlos Chagas
significance: Uniquely described the parasite, insect vector, and clinical disease of what became known as Chagas disease in a single body of work.

name: Martinus Beijerinck
significance: Isolated nitrogen-fixing root-nodule bacteria and coined the term "virus" for the filterable agent of tobacco mosaic disease.

name: Dmitri Ivanovsky
significance: Showed in 1892 that the tobacco mosaic agent passed through filters that trapped bacteria, an early step toward discovering viruses.

name: Felix d'Herelle
significance: Coined the term bacteriophage in 1917 after identifying viruses that infect and kill bacteria.

name: Sergei Winogradsky
significance: Discovered chemolithotrophy, showing certain bacteria derive energy from inorganic compounds, founding environmental microbiology.

name: Selman Waksman
significance: Coined the term antibiotic and led the team that discovered streptomycin, the first effective TB treatment; 1952 Nobel Prize.

name: Albert Schatz
significance: As a graduate student, isolated the streptomycin-producing organism in Selman Waksman's lab in 1943.

name: Paul Ehrlich
significance: Developed the concept of chemotherapy and the arsenic compound Salvarsan, the first effective treatment for syphilis.

name: Emil von Behring
significance: Co-developed the diphtheria antitoxin with Kitasato Shibasaburo, becoming the first Nobel laureate in Physiology or Medicine in 1901.

name: Ferdinand Cohn
significance: Helped establish bacteriology as a science and described bacterial endospores; mentored Robert Koch early in his career.

name: Joseph Lister
significance: Applied germ theory to surgery, introducing carbolic acid antisepsis and dramatically reducing post-operative infections.

name: Ignaz Semmelweis
significance: Showed in 1847 that hand-washing with chlorinated lime drastically reduced childbed fever, though his findings were rejected in his lifetime.

name: Edward Jenner
significance: Developed the first vaccine in 1796, using cowpox material to confer immunity against smallpox.

name: Hans Christian Gram
significance: Developed the Gram stain in 1884, still the foundational method for classifying bacteria by cell-wall structure.

name: Carl Woese
significance: Used 16S rRNA sequencing to discover Archaea as a distinct domain of life, separate from Bacteria, in 1977.

name: Karl Stetter
significance: Discovered and characterized numerous hyperthermophilic archaea, including Pyrococcus furiosus and Nanoarchaeum equitans.

name: Thomas Brock
significance: Discovered Thermus aquaticus in Yellowstone hot springs; its heat-stable enzyme later enabled the PCR method.

name: Kary Mullis
significance: Invented the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in 1983, revolutionizing molecular biology and diagnostics; 1993 Nobel Prize.

name: Rosalind Franklin
significance: Produced the X-ray diffraction data that was critical evidence for the double-helix structure of DNA.

name: Oswald Avery
significance: Co-showed in 1944 that DNA, not protein, is the molecule carrying genetic information, using pneumococcus transformation experiments.

name: Frederick Griffith
significance: Discovered bacterial transformation in 1928, showing that harmless pneumococci could acquire virulence from dead virulent ones.

name: Joshua Lederberg
significance: Discovered bacterial conjugation and named plasmids; shared the 1958 Nobel Prize for founding bacterial genetics.

name: Francoise Barre-Sinoussi
significance: Co-discovered HIV in 1983 as the cause of AIDS, sharing the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

name: Luc Montagnier
significance: Co-led the team at the Pasteur Institute that isolated HIV from a patient's lymph node in 1983.

name: Harald zur Hausen
significance: Identified high-risk human papillomavirus types as the cause of cervical cancer, earning the 2008 Nobel Prize.

name: Baruch Blumberg
significance: Discovered the hepatitis B surface antigen in 1967, leading to a diagnostic test and the first hepatitis B vaccine.

name: Peter Piot
significance: Co-discovered the Ebola virus in 1976 during an outbreak investigation in Zaire.

name: Raimond Sabouraud
significance: Founded modern medical mycology and developed Sabouraud agar, still used to culture fungi in laboratories today.

name: George Beadle
significance: Co-developed the "one gene, one enzyme" hypothesis using the mold Neurospora crassa; shared the 1958 Nobel Prize.

name: Edward Tatum
significance: Co-developed the one gene, one enzyme hypothesis with George Beadle and later worked with Joshua Lederberg on bacterial genetics.

name: Christiaan Huygens
significance: Ground lenses and made some of the earliest recorded observations of microscopic organisms, alongside his work in physics and astronomy.

name: Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg
significance: Pioneered the systematic study and naming of microscopic organisms, including many protozoa and cyanobacteria.

name: Camillo Golgi
significance: Linked the synchronized fever cycles of malaria to the parasite's blood-stage reproduction; shared the 1906 Nobel Prize for separate neuroscience work.

name: Charles Nicolle
significance: Identified the body louse as the vector of typhus and co-discovered Toxoplasma gondii; awarded the 1928 Nobel Prize.

name: Fritz Schaudinn
significance: Co-identified the spirochete bacterium that causes syphilis in 1905, shortly before his early death.

name: Karl Landsteiner
significance: Co-demonstrated that poliomyelitis is caused by a filterable virus in 1908; also discovered human blood groups, earning the 1930 Nobel Prize.

name: John Enders
significance: Co-developed methods to grow viruses in tissue culture, enabling the first isolation of measles virus and the polio vaccine; 1954 Nobel Prize.

name: Gerhard Armauer Hansen
significance: Identified the leprosy bacillus in 1873, the first bacterium ever linked to a specific human disease.

name: David Bruce
significance: Identified the bacterium causing Malta fever (brucellosis) and the trypanosome causing African sleeping sickness in livestock.

name: William Leishman
significance: Independently identified the parasite causing visceral leishmaniasis in 1900-1903, alongside Charles Donovan.

name: Kiyoshi Shiga
significance: Identified the dysentery bacillus during a major Japanese epidemic in 1898, later named Shigella in his honor.

name: Albert Neisser
significance: Identified the gonococcus bacterium in 1879, the first bacterium linked to a sexually transmitted infection.

name: Jules Bordet
significance: Co-identified the whooping cough bacterium and made foundational discoveries in immune complement systems; 1919 Nobel Prize.

name: Theodor Escherich
significance: Isolated and described Escherichia coli from infant feces in 1885, the organism later named in his honor.

name: Elie Metchnikoff
significance: Discovered phagocytosis and studied Lactobacillus fermented milk, proposing links between gut microbes and longevity; 1908 Nobel Prize.
